title: Take up your bed (Luke 5:12–26)
hook: a leper touched, and a man let through a roof by friends
carry: we have seen strange things today

segments.voice: Yesterday, a tired fisherman, a breaking net, and depart from me. Your line was fear not. When kindness came your way, did you let it land? Day five hundred twenty.

Two people today who can't get close to Jesus on their own. The first is a man "full of leprosy," as Luke puts it. In the Bible, leprosy covers a range of skin diseases, and it meant living apart, kept at a distance from family and worship. He falls on his face and says: "Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean." Not can you. If you want to. And Luke says Jesus "put forth his hand, and touched him." Before the healing, the touch. Maybe the first touch the man had felt in years. The second person is lying on a mat in a house so crowded no one can get in the door.

Jesus is teaching inside a house, and the room is packed with teachers of the law from all over, from Galilee, Judea, even Jerusalem. Some men arrive carrying their friend, who is paralyzed, on a bed. They can't get through the crowd. So they climb onto the roof. In the King James words: they "let him down through the tiling with his couch into the midst before Jesus." Picture it: dust falling, tiles lifted, a mat swaying down on ropes into the middle of a lecture. Then this line: "And when he saw their faith, he said unto him, Man, thy sins are forgiven thee." Their faith. The friends'. The man on the mat may not have said a word. His friends' faith carried him through the roof. The teachers in the room ask a serious question, and a fair one from their scriptures: "Who can forgive sins, but God alone?" Jesus answers by doing the visible thing so they'll believe the invisible one: "Arise, and take up thy couch, and go into thine house." And the man stands, picks up the bed that carried him, and walks home praising God. Then Luke's best line, the whole room in one sentence: "We have seen strange things to day." The Greek word is paradoxa, things contrary to what anyone expected. It's where English gets paradox. A man who couldn't walk carrying his own bed. A roof with a hole in it. Christians see in this scene who Jesus is. Anyone can see in it what good friends are.
screen: then, large: `WE HAVE SEEN STRANGE THINGS TO DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help someone get where they need to be. Settle, and breathe. Picture the friends on the roof, sweating, lifting tiles, lowering the ropes slowly. Now think of someone in your life who can't get where they need to be on their own right now. Someone who needs a ride to an appointment. Someone who needs an introduction, a reference, a hand with a form. Someone who needs carrying for a while, because they're too tired or too sad to walk. Let one person come to mind. Then think of the roof: is there a creative way around the crowd? A call, an errand, a door you can open. If you pray, you can carry that person to God in your mind. If you don't, simply carry them in your thoughts. The bell holds the time.
Paradoxa, Luke's Greek word for strange things, beyond all expecting: a paralyzed man's friends lower him through a roof, and he rises, takes up his own bed, and walks home praising God.
Your line: we have seen strange things today. Do the one thing that helps your person get where they need to go, and if it takes a little ingenuity, so much the better. Day five hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Many Christians point to the friends on the roof when they pray for others or help someone who can't help themselves, sometimes called carrying someone in prayer.

fork.setup: you and three friends are carrying a man on a mat. the house is packed and the door is blocked. what do you do?
options: wait outside until the crowd leaves.
climb on the roof and lower him through the tiles.
take him home and try another day.
fork.reveal: they go up on the roof, open the tiles and lower him into the middle of the room, and Jesus sees their faith.

original.note: Greek: strange things, beyond all expecting. the root of the English word paradox.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a healing.
what it means: the friends' faith brings a man through a roof, and Jesus forgives and heals him, so that the room says: strange things today.
what a scholar hears: Luke says the man was let down "through the tiling," a roof of tiles, while Mark describes digging through the roof.

notes: Biblical 'leprosy' covering various skin diseases, and the separation it required (Leviticus 13:45–46), stated generally. Confirm.
Luke 5:18 does not give the number of friends (Mark 2:3 says four); the script does not number them.
'Paradoxa' as the root of 'paradox': standard etymology.
The teachers' question is framed as a fair one from their own scriptures, not as a foil.
